facts.text: Experts have cracked a code to unlock a 400-year-old padlock found in a shipwreck.
Researchers say they now have the four-letter code that kept the mysterious lock — found among a hoard of silver coins — firmly shut for centuries.
The brass padlock had remained locked since the Ann Francis treasure hoard was found wrecked off the Welsh coast.
Peter said: “When I found the lock I was immediately astonished by the incredible workmanship and its astonishing condition.
With specialists from Cardiff University , museum experts used CT scanning technology to examine the lock’s internal mechanism without causing damage.

Senior curator for numismatics and the Welsh economy at Amgueddfa Cymru, Alastair Willis, commented: “Elizabethan combination locks are known in Britain, but this one is in exceptionally good condition and is associated with a dated wreck, making it a unique find and the code a tantalizing mystery to solve.
This scan is what allowed researchers to identify the correct letter combination: ANCE.
“We normally use this technology to study bones and other biological structures, so investigating a 400-year-old padlock was certainly a first for us.”
“When I moved the ring dials of the combination they turned with ease after over 400 years beneath the sands and I was left in disbelief,” he said.
“I also remember being left excited at the prospect of finding wonderful things from the treasure chest it once locked.”
Experts have used cutting-edge technology to open a centuries-old combination lock from one of the most “remarkable” shipwrecks found in the UK .
These scans allowed researchers to identify the correct letter combination – ANCE – and successfully unlock the historic artefact.
He added: “We normally use this technology to study bones and other biological structures, so investigating a 400-year-old padlock was certainly a first for us.”
Scientists have used cutting-edge technology to crack the four-letter code of a brass combination lock from that lay buried on a beach in Wales for more than four centuries.
The padlock forms part of the wider Ann Francis treasure hoard, which was recovered over a 21-year period between 1996 and 2017 by metal detectorist Peter Hughes.

The cracked padlock is now on public display at the National Waterfront Museum in Swansea alongside other recovered treasures, including rare gold coins from the reign of Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, and an Elizabethan boatswain's whistle.

Alastair Willis, Senior Curator for Numismatics and the Welsh Economy at Amgueddfa Cymru, said: “Elizabethan combination locks are known in Britain, but this one is in exceptionally good condition and is associated with a dated wreck, making it a unique find and the code a tantalising mystery to solve.
Researchers have cracked the four-letter combination of a brass lock that had remained secured since the 16th century, using advanced CT scanning technology to reveal the code hidden inside.
A-N-C-E. \"It's not every day you get to solve a 400-year-old mystery,\" Dr.
THE TAKEAWAY: A mystery sealed beneath the sea for more than 400 years has finally been unlocked.
